The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

items.title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest 132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

items.title: Illuminating phage dark matter beyond the reach of structural alignments with PhageFlare
items.abstract_or_text: Many phage proteins remain functionally uncharacterized despite advances in structural-similarity-based annotation. We introduce PhageFlare, a deep learning framework for predicting phage protein functions lacking significant structural matches to annotated references. Across three structure-disjoint benchmarks, where no significant Foldseek match was detected between training and test proteins (E-value thresholds of 10-3, 10-4, and 10-2), PhageFlare achieved macro-averaged F1 scores of 0.871, 0.889, and 0.738 outperforming the strongest baseline (0.789, 0.814, and 0.732). Systematic evaluations demonstrated that protein language model selection critically influences performance, with ESM-C achieving stronger overall performance than ESM-2 and ProtBert. Embedding-guided case studies revealed local structural correspondences among proteins with limited global similarity. Applied to the efam and Metagenomic Gut Virus datasets, PhageFlare annotated 38.0% and 51.8% of proteins unresolved by Foldseek, respectively. Furthermore, PhageFlare identified lysogenic potential in 1,866 prophage-designated genomes misclassified as lytic by BACPHLIP. These results show that PhageFlare complements structural-similarity-based annotation and expands functional discovery across viral dark matter.

items.title: VoroTIDE: Protein domain segmentation through independent hierarchical searches using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
items.abstract_or_text: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce VoroTIDE (Voronoi-based Two-way Independent Domain Exploration), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. VoroTIDE applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of secondary-structure elements until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, VoroTIDE achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

items.title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources. These genes encode coding for metabolite interconversion enzymes (20%), transporters (15%), and protein-modifying enzymes (11%). Furthermore, the network analysis identified 19 subnetworks with more than two nodes and 125 unique genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed convergence of processes including action potential, synaptic function, nervous system development, TOR signaling, cilium organization, DNA repair, and cell fate specification. We identified 44 first-order neighbors connecting the subnetworks. By integrating drug-target interactions from DrugBank using CyTargetLinker, we highlighted potential therapeutic targets within the S4 subnetwork, associated with cerebral cortex development, as well as CREB1, a connector between subnetworks. Conclusion: Network analysis organized heterogeneous epilepsy-associated genes into biologically related subnetworks and generated hypotheses for further research.

items.title: Ligand-Based Design of Lyn-Selective Type II Kinase Inhibitors by Rational Tail Modification of Imatinib
items.abstract_or_text: Lyn is a tyrosine kinase that plays critical roles in immune signaling and neurodegenerative diseases but is difficult to target selectively because of high homology within the Src-family of kinases. Here, we report ligand-based optimization of the type II inhibitor imatinib through systematic tail modification to enhance Lyn potency and selectivity. This approach yielded potent inhibitors, including compound 22 with low-nanomolar Lyn inhibition and compound 27 with 500-fold selectivity over Hck. Compound 22 showed a limited off-target kinase profile under low-ATP conditions that was further narrowed at 1 mM ATP while retaining submicromolar Lyn inhibition. Complementary 3D-QSAR and Markov state modeling linked tail-region steric features to ligand-dependent activation-loop conformational ensembles. In human microglia, 22 suppressed Aβ-induced Lyn autophosphorylation and increased CD163 high CLEC7A high DAM-like and Aβ-positive DAM-like populations. These findings establish compound 22 as a novel molecular probe for interrogating Lyn catalytic function across diverse disease-relevant contexts.

items.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
items.abstract_or_text: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

items.title: BigFingerprint: A Topology-aware Extended-connectivity Fingerprint for Polymers
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning-driven polymer design and property prediction require molecular representations that encode not only local chemistry but also the statistically distributed monomer sequences and connectivity patterns and global topology that distinguish polymers from small molecules. Existing fingerprinting workflows often fail to capture global polymer architecture, as well as connectivity across repeat units, end groups, and linking groups. This work develops BigFingerprint, a topology-aware extended-connectivity fingerprint for polymers represented by BigSMILES. BigFingerprint consists of two components, a polymer extended-connectivity fingerprint, p-ECFP, that encodes atom-centered substructures within and across stochastic molecular fragments, and a polymer topology fingerprint, p-TFP, that encodes global architectural features such as block, statistical, graft, star, branched, and network topologies. Through representative structural examples and polymer property prediction tasks, BigFingerprint retains the chemical interpretability of circular fingerprints while extending their applicability to complex polymer architectures. As a critical component of the BigSMILES-centered ecosystem, BigFingerprint integrates local substructural information with global topological descriptors to provide a general and chemically interpretable representation for substructure analysis, similarity

items.title: Diastereoselective synthesis of glycosyl-1-thiophosphates as reporters for nucleotide diphosphate sugar metabolism
items.abstract_or_text: Glycosylation controls key physiological processes such as cell-cell recognition, signal transduction, and protein folding/trafficking within subcellular compartments. Glycans are often assembled by Leloir glycosyltransferase enzymes, which use nucleotide diphosphate monosaccharides (NDP-monosaccharides) as substrates. Cells produce NDP-monosaccharides through metabolic transformation of corresponding glycosyl-1-phosphates (G1Ps). Existing LC-MS-based approaches to study NDP-monosaccharide metabolism in living cells are limited due to the mass degeneracy of the epimeric physiological pyranoses that populate the NDP-monosaccharide pool. Technology that enables tracking of NDP-monosaccharide metabolism from chemically defined metabolic precursors would illuminate these challenging-to-study pathways that are central to immunity, signal transduction, and cellular homeostasis. To circumvent this challenge, we have developed a series of cell-permeable glycosyl-1- thio phosphates (G1TPs) in which a single oxygen atom is replaced with a sulphur atom at the phosphorus centre. This chalcogen substitution generated a mass-unique signature that enabled tracking of select NDP-monosaccharide metabolites. To generate G1TPs, we leveraged a cyclic thiophosphorochloridate reagent to selectively install a 1,3,2-dioxaphospholane group at the anomeric centre of per- O -acetyl-D-pyranoses. Our approach included anomeric stereocontrol, which provided access to both native (α) and non-physiological (β) diastereomers at C1. Next, we leveraged the intrinsic strain of the dioxaphospholane system to efficiently install an S -acetyl-2-thioethyl (SATE) group by direct ring opening with thioacetate. LC-MS analysis confirmed that the resultant per- O -Ac- and SATE-protected G1TPs were cell permeable and could be deprotected to free G1TPs once inside. Importantly, metabolomic analysis revealed that an archetypal G1TP – α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate – was metabolized to the corresponding NDP-(S)-galactose in cellulo , whereas the β-counterpart was not. Finally, we demonstrated that α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate G1TP was non-toxic, did not perturb native glycan biosynthesis, and did not impact gene transcription. Combined, these results establish G1TPs as biologically silent reporters for NDP-monosaccharide metabolism.

items.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation
items.abstract_or_text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.

items.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
items.abstract_or_text: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding 1/2 in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce neural triage decoding, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the Triage decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

items.title: AegisFlow: Training-Free Non-Myopic Path-Safe Guided Flow Matching
items.abstract_or_text: Pretrained generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching models, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in synthesizing high-quality data. However, steering their generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints--such as identity preservation in image editing or obstacle avoidance in robotics--remains fundamentally challenging. While recent training-free guidance methods enforce path-safety, they rely heavily on min-norm controllers that only account for immediate constraint satisfaction. These myopic approaches often yield suboptimal trajectories that hover dangerously close to the boundary, severely restricting the model's ability to optimize toward its target. In this paper, we propose AegisFlow, a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that recasts guided generation as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope. By integrating a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional, AegisFlow naturally enforces constraints along the entire generative path. To compute the global optimal control, we derive a tractable, mathematically grounded approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods across text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning, establishing a significantly better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction. Code is available at https://github.com/LiuKunpeng03/AegisFlow.

items.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
items.abstract_or_text: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.
